title: Gross Anatomy I: Upper and Lower Limbs (ANA 201)
description: Bones, muscles, joints, nerves and vessels of the upper and lower limbs, with their clinical applications.

topics.title: Pectoral Region, Axilla and Brachial Plexus
topics.summary: Muscles of the pectoral region, boundaries and contents of the axilla, and the brachial plexus with its injuries.

notes.b: The axilla is a pyramidal space between the arm and the chest wall. Its apex (cervico-axillary canal) is bounded by the clavicle, first rib and upper border of the scapula; the anterior wall is formed by pectoralis major and minor; the posterior wall by subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi; the medial wall by serratus anterior over the ribs; the lateral wall by the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. Contents: axillary artery and vein, cords and branches of the brachial plexus, axillary lymph nodes (five groups: anterior/pectoral, posterior/subscapular, lateral/humeral, central, apical) and fat.
k: Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts
Apical nodes receive lymph from all other groups
Breast lymph drains mainly to the anterior (pectoral) nodes

notes.b: The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C5–T1 and is organised as roots, trunks (upper C5–6, middle C7, lower C8–T1), divisions and cords (lateral, posterior, medial, named relative to the axillary artery). Terminal branches: musculocutaneous (lateral cord), median (lateral + medial cords), ulnar (medial cord), axillary and radial (posterior cord). Erb–Duchenne palsy (C5–6, upper trunk, e.g. difficult delivery) produces the 'waiter's tip' position; Klumpke's palsy (C8–T1, lower trunk) causes claw hand and may be accompanied by Horner's syndrome. Injury to the long thoracic nerve (C5–7) paralyses serratus anterior, causing a winged scapula.
k: Roots C5–T1; mnemonic: Real Teachers Drink Cold Beer

q: The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of:
The plexus arises from C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1.
Erb's palsy results from injury to the:
Upper trunk injury gives the 'waiter's tip' posture.
A winged scapula follows injury to the nerve supplying:
The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior.
The axillary artery is divided into three parts by:
Pectoralis minor crosses the artery, defining its three parts.
The ulnar nerve arises from the:
The ulnar nerve is the terminal continuation of the medial cord.
Which nerve arises from the posterior cord?
The posterior cord gives the axillary and radial nerves.
Most lymph from the breast drains to the ___ axillary nodes.
About 75% of breast lymph goes to the anterior (pectoral) nodes.
Klumpke's palsy may be associated with Horner's syndrome because of injury to:
T1 carries preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head.

topics.title: Arm, Forearm and Hand
topics.summary: Compartments, cubital fossa, carpal tunnel and the major nerve injuries of the upper limb.

notes.b: The anterior compartment of the arm (biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis) is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve; the posterior compartment (triceps) by the radial nerve. The cubital fossa is bounded by a line between the humeral epicondyles above, brachioradialis laterally and pronator teres medially. From lateral to medial it contains the biceps tendon, the brachial artery and the median nerve (mnemonic 'TAN'). Forearm flexors are mainly supplied by the median nerve (except flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus — ulnar); extensors by the radial (posterior interosseous) nerve.
k: Cubital fossa (lateral → medial): Tendon, Artery, Nerve
FCU and medial FDP: ulnar nerve

notes.b: The carpal tunnel, formed by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum, transmits the median nerve and nine tendons (FDS ×4, FDP ×4, FPL). Carpal tunnel syndrome compresses the median nerve, causing thenar wasting and paraesthesia of the lateral three and a half digits. The median nerve supplies the LOAF muscles of the hand (lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis); the ulnar nerve supplies the remaining intrinsic muscles. Radial nerve injury in the spiral groove (midshaft humerus fracture) causes wrist drop; ulnar nerve injury causes a claw hand; median injury at the elbow causes the 'hand of benediction'. The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone and risks avascular necrosis.
k: Midshaft humerus fracture → radial nerve → wrist drop

q: From lateral to medial, the contents of the cubital fossa are:
Biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve
Median nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery
Radial nerve, ulnar nerve, median nerve
Mnemonic TAN: Tendon, Artery, Nerve from lateral to medial.
Wrist drop follows a fracture of the humerus at the:
The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove.
Which nerve is compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome?
The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel.
The most commonly fractured carpal bone is the:
Scaphoid fractures follow falls on the outstretched hand.
Which hand muscle is supplied by the median nerve?
The median nerve supplies the LOAF muscles, including abductor pollicis brevis.
The muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm are supplied by the:
Biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis are supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.
A claw hand deformity is classically due to injury of the:
Ulnar nerve palsy paralyses most intrinsic hand muscles.
Flexor carpi ulnaris is supplied by the:
FCU and the medial half of FDP are the ulnar-supplied forearm flexors.

topics.title: Shoulder, Elbow and Wrist Joints
topics.summary: Joint types, the rotator cuff, dislocations and the joints of the upper limb.

notes.b: The glenohumeral joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket synovial joint with a shallow glenoid cavity deepened by the glenoid labrum. It is highly mobile but relatively unstable; stability comes mainly from the rotator cuff (SITS): supraspinatus (abduction, first 15°), infraspinatus and teres minor (lateral rotation), subscapularis (medial rotation). Most dislocations are anterior (inferior), and can injure the axillary nerve, which supplies deltoid and teres minor and gives sensation over the 'regimental badge' area.

The elbow is a hinge joint (humero-ulnar and humeroradial); the proximal radio-ulnar joint is a pivot joint allowing pronation and supination, with the radial head held by the annular ligament ('pulled elbow' in toddlers is subluxation of the radial head). The wrist (radiocarpal) is a condyloid (ellipsoid) joint. A fall on the outstretched hand in the elderly causes a Colles' fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement ('dinner-fork deformity').
k: Pulled elbow: radial head slips out of the annular ligament

q: Which muscle initiates abduction of the shoulder?
Supraspinatus initiates the first 15° of abduction.
The rotator cuff muscle that medially rotates the arm is:
Subscapularis is the only cuff muscle producing medial rotation.
The nerve at risk in anterior dislocation of the shoulder is the:
The axillary nerve winds round the surgical neck of the humerus.
The proximal radio-ulnar joint is a:
It allows rotation for pronation and supination.
The ligament that holds the radial head is the:
The annular ligament encircles the radial head.
Colles' fracture has dorsal displacement of the distal radius.
The shoulder joint is classified as a:
The glenohumeral joint is a ball-and-socket synovial joint.
The fibrocartilaginous rim that deepens the glenoid cavity is the:
The glenoid labrum increases the depth of the socket.

topics.title: Gluteal Region, Thigh and Femoral Triangle
topics.summary: Gluteal muscles and the sciatic nerve, the femoral triangle, and thigh compartments.

notes.b: Gluteus maximus (inferior gluteal nerve) extends and laterally rotates the hip — important in climbing stairs and rising from sitting. Gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve) abduct the hip and stabilise the pelvis during walking; their paralysis produces a positive Trendelenburg sign (the pelvis drops on the unsupported side). The sciatic nerve (L4–S3) leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis. Intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid the sciatic nerve.
k: Inject in the upper outer quadrant

notes.b: The femoral triangle is bounded by the inguinal ligament (superiorly), sartorius (laterally) and adductor longus (medially). From lateral to medial its contents are the femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein and the empty space/Lymphatics in the femoral canal (NAVEL). Femoral hernias pass through the femoral canal, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and are more common in women. Anterior thigh muscles (quadriceps, sartorius) are supplied by the femoral nerve; medial (adductors) by the obturator nerve; posterior (hamstrings) by the sciatic nerve.
k: Femoral hernia: through the femoral canal
Anterior thigh: femoral; medial: obturator; posterior: sciatic

q: A positive Trendelenburg sign indicates weakness of:
These hip abductors stabilise the pelvis during single-leg stance.
From lateral to medial, the femoral triangle contains the femoral:
Mnemonic NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, (Empty space), Lymphatics.
The lateral boundary of the femoral triangle is:
Gluteal intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant to avoid the:
The sciatic nerve lies in the lower medial part of the buttock.
The adductor muscles of the thigh are mainly supplied by the:
The obturator nerve supplies the medial compartment.
The hamstrings are supplied by the:
The tibial division of the sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings.
Gluteus maximus is supplied by the:
The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus.
The main action of gluteus maximus is:
It is the powerful hip extensor used in climbing and rising.

topics.title: Knee, Leg, Ankle and Foot
topics.summary: The knee joint, compartments of the leg, foot drop and arches of the foot.

notes.b: The knee is a modified hinge synovial joint. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) prevents anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur (anterior drawer test); the posterior cruciate ligament prevents posterior displacement. The medial meniscus is C-shaped and attached to the tibial (medial) collateral ligament, so it is injured more often than the lateral meniscus. The 'unhappy triad' (O'Donoghue) is injury to the ACL, medial collateral ligament and medial meniscus. Popliteus 'unlocks' the extended knee.
k: Medial meniscus is fixed to the MCL — injured more

notes.b: The anterior compartment of the leg (tibialis anterior, extensors) is supplied by the deep fibular (peroneal) nerve; the lateral compartment (fibularis longus and brevis — eversion) by the superficial fibular nerve; the posterior compartment (gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior) by the tibial nerve. The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, where it is easily injured (e.g. tight plaster cast), causing foot drop with a high-stepping gait. The foot has medial and lateral longitudinal arches and a transverse arch; the talus bears the body's weight and has no muscle attachments. The ankle jerk tests S1.
k: Common fibular nerve at the fibular neck → foot drop
Deep fibular: dorsiflexion; superficial fibular: eversion
Ankle jerk = S1; knee jerk = L3–L4

q: The anterior drawer test assesses the:
Excess anterior tibial translation indicates an ACL tear.
Foot drop commonly follows injury to the common fibular nerve at the:
It winds superficially around the fibular neck.
Which meniscus is more commonly injured?
The medial meniscus is attached to the MCL and is less mobile.
Eversion of the foot is produced mainly by muscles supplied by the:
Fibularis longus and brevis in the lateral compartment evert the foot.
The muscle that 'unlocks' the fully extended knee is:
Popliteus laterally rotates the femur on the tibia to unlock the knee.
The ankle jerk reflex tests nerve root:
The Achilles reflex is mediated mainly by S1.
Tibialis anterior is supplied by the:
The deep fibular nerve supplies the anterior compartment (dorsiflexors).
The 'unhappy triad' of the knee includes injury to the ACL, MCL and:
O'Donoghue's triad: ACL, MCL and medial meniscus.
